It's January 1960. Two men are sealed inside a tiny steel sphere, sinking to the deepest point on Earth, nearly eleven kilometers down. The pressure out there could crush a car like a soda can. And strapped to the outside of the sub... is a wristwatch. When they came back up, it was still ticking perfectly. The company behind it was started by an orphan, got its name on a bus ride, and today is owned by... a charity. This is the story of Rolex.

Hans Wilsdorf was born in Germany in 1881. By the age of twelve, he had lost both of his parents. But he was brilliant with languages and numbers, and he landed a job at a watch exporter in Switzerland, the heart of the watch world. Back then, real gentlemen carried pocket watches. Wristwatches were seen as tiny, fragile jewelry, and most people thought they were a passing fad. Hans was sure they were the future.

In 1905, at just twenty-four, he started a watch company in London with his brother-in-law. The name? Wilsdorf and Davis. Not exactly catchy. Worse, jewelers stamped their own names on his watches, so nobody knew who made them. Hans needed a name that was short, easy to say in any language, and small enough to fit on a dial. According to Hans, it came to him on top of a London omnibus, as if a genie had whispered it in his ear. Rolex. He registered it in 1908.

To prove wristwatches weren't toys, he went after hard evidence. In 1910, a Rolex became the first wristwatch to earn an official Swiss chronometer certificate. In 1914, Britain's Kew Observatory gave one a top precision rating, an honor usually reserved for big marine chronometers that steered ships. Then World War One brought heavy taxes on imported luxuries, so in 1919 Hans moved the company to Geneva, Switzerland, where it has stayed ever since.

But wristwatches still had a deadly enemy: water and dust. So in 1926, Rolex created the Oyster, a sealed case with a screw-down crown, and the first truly waterproof wristwatch case. To prove it, a young swimmer named Mercedes Gleitze wore one during an attempt to cross the English Channel in 1927. She spent over ten hours in freezing water. She didn't make it all the way across, but the watch kept perfect time.

Hans bought the entire front page of a London newspaper to brag about it. Then he gave jewelers aquariums, with watches ticking away underwater right in the shop window. People stopped on the street just to stare. Four years later, in 1931, Rolex invented the Perpetual rotor, a little weight that winds the watch every time you move your arm. Here's a story most people have never heard. During World War Two, captured British pilots often had their watches taken away by the guards. Hans made them an incredible offer: order a Rolex from your prison camp, and pay for it after the war. Thousands of orders came in. He was betting that these men would survive, and that their side would win. For the prisoners, that bet meant everything.

After the war, Rolex turned the whole planet into its testing lab. In 1953, the expedition that first conquered Mount Everest was equipped with Rolex watches. That same year came the Submariner, a watch built for divers. Then the GMT-Master for airline pilots, and the Day-Date, so popular with world leaders that it was nicknamed the President. And in 1960, that watch strapped to the Trieste came back from the bottom of the ocean, still running.

Now for the twist. Hans's wife died in 1944, and the couple had no children. So he created the Hans Wilsdorf Foundation, and when he died in 1960, his shares went to it. That means Rolex has no stock, no shareholders, and nobody who can buy it. It even makes its own gold in its own foundry. And today, every new Rolex is tested to stay accurate within two seconds a day.

So what's the most famous Rolex of all? In 1963, Rolex launched the Daytona, a racing chronograph that barely sold at first. Then actor Paul Newman started wearing one, a gift from his wife, engraved with three words: Drive Carefully Me. In 2017, experts guessed it might fetch a million dollars at auction. It sold for seventeen point eight million. The watch nobody wanted became the one everybody wanted. Which fact surprised you the most?
